blocks.text: Kidney (renal) failure is a condition in which the kidneys lose their ability to filter wastes from the blood and to regulate the body's fluid and salt balance.

blocks.caption: Chronic and acute kidney failure
rows: diabetes, high blood pressure, kidney disease such as chronic infection or inflammation of the glomeruli
kidney infection; blockage of the urinary tract by stones, bladder cancer or an enlarged prostate; some medicines such as NSAIDs; blood clots in the renal arteries or arterioles

blocks.text: Renal dialysis treats kidney failure by filtering metabolic wastes from the blood by artificial means. There are two general types, haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis.

items: Haemodialysis: blood is circulated outside the body through a dialyzer, a filter containing a semipermeable membrane made of cellulose. A catheter is put into an artery, usually in the arm; the blood passes through the dialyzer, which also holds a special fluid, the dialysate. Wastes, water and salts pass from the blood through the membrane and dissolve in the dialysate, and the cleaned blood returns to the body through a second catheter in a vein.

Peritoneal dialysis uses the peritoneal membrane that lines the abdominal cavity. 1.5 to 2 L of dialysate is run into the abdomen through a catheter and left for 4 to 6 hours; wastes and extra fluid pass from the capillaries of the peritoneum into it. The dialysate is then drained and discarded, and the process is repeated several times a day.

blocks.alt: Four panels. Breaking kidney stones: a lithotripter outside the body sends shockwaves to a stone (ECSWL), and for larger stones a tube from the back lets a nephroscope and ultrasound break and remove it (PNL). A table of stone types with their cause and urine test. Haemodialysis: blood from an artery pumped through a dialyzer with a cellulose membrane, dialysate flowing the other way, clean blood back to a vein. Peritoneal dialysis: dialysate run into the abdomen, left, then drained.
blocks.caption: Haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis (original diagram after Figures 14.7 and 14.8).
blocks.long_description: About 70% of stones are calcium oxalate (from high calcium and oxalate in urine; the urine is acidic), about 10% uric acid (from high uric acid in the blood; the urine stays acidic), and others calcium phosphate (alkaline urine) or cystine and phosphates; continued dehydration raises the risk. Stones are broken by lithotripsy: shockwaves from outside the body (ECSWL) or, for larger stones, a nephroscope and ultrasound through a tube in the back (PNL). In haemodialysis blood passes a semipermeable cellulose membrane with dialysate on the other side, so wastes, extra water and salts cross into it; the two flow in opposite directions to keep a gradient all along. In peritoneal dialysis 1.5 to 2 L of dialysate stays in the abdomen for 4 to 6 hours, collecting wastes through the peritoneum, and is drained several times a day.

items: Access to the bloodstream raises the risk of infection.
Hypotension (low blood pressure) is a common complication of haemodialysis.
Muscle cramps can occur because salt levels change.
Dialysis can cause anaemia, leading to fatigue and weakness.
Removing too much fluid too quickly can cause dehydration or low blood pressure.
Treatment can be emotionally hard; patients may feel anxious, depressed or overwhelmed.

blocks.title: Why opposite directions?
blocks.text: In the dialyzer, blood and dialysate flow in opposite directions. All along the membrane the dialysate meeting the blood is fresher than the blood, so wastes keep diffusing out over the whole length instead of the two fluids levelling off halfway.

blocks.prompt: Compare haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis: what acts as the filter in each?
blocks.explanation: In haemodialysis the filter is the cellulose semipermeable membrane of the dialyzer outside the body; in peritoneal dialysis it is the patient's own peritoneum, the membrane lining the abdomen.

items: Chronic failure: slow, irreversible (diabetes, high blood pressure); acute: sudden, often treatable (infection, blockage, NSAIDs, clots).
Haemodialysis: dialyzer with cellulose membrane, counter-flow dialysate. Peritoneal: 1.5 to 2 L in the abdomen for 4 to 6 h. Risks: infection, low blood pressure, cramps, anaemia.
